canonical_examples.problem: What is the sum of the series $\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{(\pi/3)^3}{3!} + \dfrac{(\pi/3)^5}{5!}-\cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n}(\pi/3)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+\cdots\,?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = \sin x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯\,\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{(\pi /3)^{3}}{3!}+\frac{(\pi /3)^{5}}{5!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}(\pi /3)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯ \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{(\pi /3)^{3}}{3!}+\frac{(\pi /3)^{5}}{5!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}(\pi /3)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

Example: 
                    Recognizing Series That Are Similar to the Maclaurin Expansion for Cosine
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = \cos x.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=1-\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{4!}{x}^{4}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}\,{x}^{2n}}{(2n)!}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=3$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3) & =1-\frac{{3}^{2}}{2!}+\frac{{3}^{4}}{4!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{3}^{2n}}{(2n)!}\,⋯ \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3) & =1-\frac{9}{2!}+\frac{81}{4!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{3}^{2n}}{(2n)!}\,⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\cos(3).$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We need to recognize when a particular series looks like a standard Maclaurin series. A list of some common Maclaurin series is given below.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{1-x}=1+x+{x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{n}+⋯={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{x}^{n}, &  & x\in (-1,1) \\  & \frac{1}{1+x}=1-x+{x}^{2}-⋯+(-1)^{n}{x}^{n}+⋯={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(-1)^{n}{x}^{n}, &  & x\in (-1,1) \\  & {e}^{x}=1+x+\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+⋯+\frac{{x}^{n}}{n!}+⋯={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{n!}, &  & x\in (-\infty ,\infty ) \\  & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)=x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n+1}{x}^{n}}{n}+⋯={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}{x}^{n}}{n}, &  & x\in (-1,1] \\  & \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)=x-\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{5!}{x}^{5}+⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}, &  & x\in (-\infty ,\infty ) \\  & \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)=1-\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{4!}{x}^{4}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{2n}}{(2n)!}+⋯={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{2n}}{(2n)!}, &  & x\in (-\infty ,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

In this lesson, we will focus on recognizing the standard Maclaurin series for the sine and cosine functions.

**Note:** To remember the series for $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ easily, notice that they are both alternating series that contain every other term of the expansion for $e^x.$ Sine has the odd-degree terms (since it is an odd function), and cosine has the even-degree terms (since it is an even function).
